questions.question: How do flowering plants primarily reproduce?
options: Asexually through runners only
Sexually through flowers
By binary fission
By producing spores

questions.question: In flowering plants, what are the female gametes called?
options: Pollen grains
Anthers
Egg cells (ova)
Zygotes

questions.question: What structures in flowering plants carry the male gametes?
options: Pollen grains
Ovaries
Stigmas
Petals

questions.question: Which part of a seed-producing plant matures and ripens to become a fruit?
options: The anther
The pollen tube
The petal
The ovary

questions.question: Which group of animals represents the largest and most common group of plant pollinators?
options: Birds
Bats
Bees
Butterflies

questions.question: What is meant by the term 'food security'?
options: Protecting agricultural fields from wild animals
Having enough affordable and nutritious food in an area or country
Storing seeds in a secure underground vault
Using chemicals to preserve food for many years

questions.question: Which of the following describes the process of pollination?
options: The fusion of the male and female nuclei
The movement of seeds away from the parent plant
The transfer of pollen from the male anther to the female stigma
The growth of a pollen tube down into the ovary

questions.question: What is a key benefit of cross-pollination compared to self-pollination?
options: It requires less energy from the plant
It increases variation within a species
It guarantees that offspring will be identical to the parent
It does not rely on any external pollinators

questions.question: In plant reproduction, how is fertilisation defined?
options: The release of pollen into the air
The transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma
The germination of a seed on damp cotton wool
The fusion of the nuclei from the male and the female gametes

questions.question: What is the correct sequence of development after fertilisation in plants?
options: An embryo becomes a zygote, which then becomes a seed coat
A zygote grows into an embryo, which then grows into a new plant
A pollen grain becomes a zygote, which directly forms a fruit
An egg cell becomes an embryo, which then becomes a zygote

questions.question: If you are investigating the effect of different types of soil on seed germination, which graph type should you use and why?
options: A line graph, because soil type is a continuous variable
A bar chart, because soil type is a categoric variable
A line graph, because soil type is a categoric variable
A bar chart, because soil type is a continuous variable

questions.question: Which adaptations would you expect to find on a seed that is dispersed by the wind?
options: Heavy weight and a sticky outer hook
Brightly coloured flesh and a sweet taste
Light weight and a large surface area
A hard shell that can float on water

questions.question: During an investigation, why is it important to repeat measurements for each value of the independent variable?
options: To ensure the dependent variable becomes a control variable
To change the values of the independent variable halfway through
To make the experiment take longer and look more professional
To identify anomalous results and calculate a mean

questions.question: Why is it important to identify and keep control variables the same in a seed germination investigation?
options: To ensure that any differences in results are due only to the independent variable
To make sure the seeds germinate as fast as possible
To allow multiple independent variables to be changed at once
To guarantee that all seeds survive without needing water

questions.question: Which of the following is a common seed used in school labs that can germinate on damp cotton wool without soil?
options: Oak acorns
Cress seeds
Coconut seeds
Apple seeds
